title: Don't Adapt to the Immature
author: Foundation Father
summary: This piece argues that the contemporary concept of empathy has been inverted into a tool the immature use to escape accountability, both within families and in wider culture, by treating any negative feeling as if it were self-evidently caused by another person's words or standards rather than by the listener's own failure to self-regulate. The author draws a sharp distinction between words hurting and words causing damage, arguing that labeling speech as 'violence' lets a person offload responsibility for their own emotional reaction onto whoever spoke. Using an extended anecdote about a father repeatedly picking a tantrum-throwing toddler up off an airport floor for twenty-five minutes, the piece contends that indulgent 'niceness' toward immaturity produces no peace and no growth, and reframes a firmer, even physically corrective response as the truer form of empathy because it accounts for who that child becomes as an adult. It closes by arguing that leadership -- explicitly including leadership of one's own family -- requires refusing to be governed by other people's feelings, since 'feelings are not an opinion' and cannot legitimately veto disagreement.
points: The essay's core distinction -- 'words may hurt, but they do not cause damage' -- is used to argue that framing speech as 'violence' functions rhetorically to transfer responsibility for an emotional reaction from the person having it onto whoever spoke, removing any incentive toward self-regulation.

The extended airport anecdote (a father who repeatedly picks his tantruming son up off the floor for twenty-five minutes) is offered as proof that indulgent responsiveness to immaturity produces neither peace nor growth, only a longer tantrum.

The piece redefines 'true empathy' as accounting for the adult the child will become, explicitly framing physical correction as more genuinely loving than permissiveness because it spares a larger, later pain.

Its leadership claim generalizes beyond parenting: refusing to be 'tyrannized by someone else's sensitivities' is presented as a requirement of leading anything, including a family, because unmanaged feelings are treated by the immature person as equivalent to an argument.
quotes: Those who are immature remain immature, and everyone else adapts around them. It is a power tool in the hands of the overly sensitive. They hurl accusations, take a fall, and everyone scrambles to calm them down.
The labels imply damage. Words may hurt, but they do not cause damage. There is a big difference. It is another way for the listener to not take responsibility for their own feelings.

If you are to be a leader, including the leader of your own family, you must refuse to be tyrannized by someone else's sensitivities. They can disagree with your opinion. They may not hurl accusations.

This fool of a father was practicing the modern version of empathy, encouraging his son to remain weak and immature. His passiveness or "niceness" might have been intended to keep the peace, but there was no peace.
and so you spank them now to spare them that future pain. He will be sad for a minute, but the bitter taste of that medicine will fade quickly.
But you were not tyrannized by their sensibilities, and as a result, your family will be better off in the long run.
